segment_name: The Vanstone Sisters: A Family Shattered

questions.question: Caroline, you said Collins makes you *feel* trapped, not just understand that these women are trapped—that the sentences themselves accelerate and become more clipped when constraint closes in. Can you actually read us a passage that does that, and walk us through what's happening on the line level?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to do close reading of sensory/physical constraint passages and establish the emotional register of the segment early

questions.question: James, I want to push on something. You're describing a blueprint of injustice, a legal machine grinding along. But Caroline's just shown us Collins working at the level of individual sentences and bodies. Is there a tension there? Can a novel be a structural indictment and an intimate emotional experience at the same time, or does emphasizing the machinery actually flatten the sisters into victims?
questions.intent: Set up the structural-vs-emotional disagreement between James and Caroline, force James to either defend or complicate his 'blueprint' framing

questions.question: Eleanor, you've got this striking claim that Collins is doing something almost modernist—that the narrative fragmentation isn't just what happens *to* the sisters, it's baked into how the narration itself works. Can you find us the moment in the opening pages where you first feel that? Where the narrator's eye catches on something before the plot has even told us what we're looking at?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to quote the opening descriptive passage and make the case for formal experimentation, setting up her 'illegitimate narrative' argument

questions.question: James, Eleanor is essentially saying this novel is formally radical—that the *structure* is illegitimate, not just the characters. You've been pretty insistent this is about legal and institutional architecture. Does formal experimentation matter to your reading at all, or is that the kind of literary criticism that actually obscures what Collins was doing politically?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement between James and Eleanor on whether formal analysis illuminates or distracts from social critique

questions.question: Caroline, both Eleanor and James are circling around the sisters as a unit—the split, the separation, the parallel trajectories. But you've said the bond between Nora and Magdalen is the emotional core that everything else pivots on. Is there a moment—maybe a passage where they touch or go silent together—where you think Collins is saying something about female solidarity that he simply couldn't say directly? Something that would've been unsayable in 1862?
questions.intent: Draw out Caroline's strongest take on the sisters' relationship as the novel's real subject, invite Eleanor and James to respond to the claim that love between the sisters outweighs both the formal experiment and the legal critique

steering_notes: The central tension in this segment is a three-way pull: Eleanor wants formal experiment, James wants institutional critique, Caroline wants emotional interiority. The most productive moments will come when you force them to account for each other's evidence rather than talk past it. Don't let James retreat into legal history without making him engage with specific sentences. Don't let Eleanor's formalism float free of what the novel actually feels like to read. The goal by the end of the segment is to have all three agree on *what* the sisters' illegitimacy costs them—and sharply disagree on *how* Collins makes that cost legible to the reader.
cross_engagement_targets: James's 'blueprint of injustice' framing directly challenges Caroline's claim that the novel is 'a love story between two sisters'—these are not obviously compatible readings and the host should name that tension explicitly

Eleanor's claim that the narrative withholds information as a form of showing the sisters' resistance rather than helplessness cuts against James's reading of them as products of institutional erasure—ask Eleanor to push back on James directly on this point

Caroline's attention to physical/sensory language and Eleanor's formalism are actually complementary rather than opposed, but neither panelist seems to have noticed—a moment where you point this out could produce a productive synthesis rather than debate

James's insistence that there is no third way (complicity or ruin) is directly challenged by Eleanor's argument that Collins encodes resistance in the narrative structure itself—this is the sharpest latent disagreement in the room

segment_name: Bastards, Heiresses, and the Law: Social Structures on Trial

questions.question: Caroline, you described the moment Nora discovers her illegitimacy as the law 'entering her body.' Can you find that passage and read it to us? Because I want everyone to actually hear it before we start debating what Collins is doing — I have a feeling we'll all be arguing about very different things once it's in the room.
questions.intent: Anchor the discussion in a specific passage; let the text do emotional work before the analytical argument begins; gives Woodcourt her strongest ground first

questions.question: James, you called this 'documentary realism disguised as sensation fiction' — which is a genuinely provocative claim. Because most people pick this book up as a thriller. So make the case: when you read that passage Caroline just read, what are you actually seeing? Legal machinery? Plot convenience? Something else?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to articulate his strongest take — that the law here is functioning as designed, not as villain — and set up direct friction with Woodcourt's emotional reading and Hartley's formal reading

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on something. James is saying Collins is exposing the law as it actually operated. Caroline is saying we feel it through Nora's devastation. But you've argued the real radicalism is *formal* — that the way Collins rations information about Magdalen and Nora's status IS itself the indictment. Can you show us what you mean in the text? Because I'm not sure James and Caroline are going to buy it until they see it.
questions.intent: Force Hartley to demonstrate her formal argument with evidence rather than assertion; creates a three-way tension between legal-historical, emotional-psychological, and narratological readings; sets up productive disagreement

questions.question: James, here's something I want to put to the table: you said Magdalen's resourcefulness — all her scheming, her disguises, Captain Wragge — only exists because legitimate options were foreclosed by law. But Caroline's been making a case for Collins's secondary characters being trapped by the same systems they perpetuate. Does Captain Wragge let your argument off the hook, or does he actually prove it?
questions.intent: Triangulate between Blackstone's systemic reading and Woodcourt's more sympathetic character reading; Wragge is a useful test case because he's both complicit in and victimized by social structures; should provoke a genuinely interesting three-way disagreement

questions.question: Last question, and I want all three of you on this one: James, you said the injustice never gets resolved — Nora and Magdalen survive the system, they don't fix it. Caroline, you said the social structure in this novel is 'animate — it breathes, it hunts, it erases people.' Eleanor, you've said Collins refuses sentiment in favour of formal structures that make us complicit. So here's the question for Caroline to start: is there any moment in this novel where a character — not the plot, not Collins, but a character — actually *sees* the system clearly and says so out loud? Or does Collins deny us even that?
questions.intent: Force all three experts to converge on the novel's political and moral stance; tests whether Collins offers any foothold of resistance or clear-eyed critique within the fiction itself; designed to produce disagreement about whether the novel is ultimately despairing or radical

steering_notes: This segment has the richest potential for genuine three-way friction. The key fault line isn't Blackstone vs the others — it's actually Woodcourt and Hartley, who both want to resist Blackstone's 'legal machinery' framing but for opposite reasons: Woodcourt wants the emotional, felt experience; Hartley wants the formal-structural argument. Watch for moments where they accidentally agree with Blackstone while arguing with each other. Keep pressing for specific passages — all three experts have strong textual instincts and the discussion will get abstract fast without anchoring. Don't let Blackstone dominate the legal-historical ground unchallenged: Woodcourt's 'the sound of Victorian legal prose is suffocating' is a direct and interesting counter to his framing, and Hartley's narratological argument is a genuine third way that could reframe the whole debate.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone says Magdalen's agency is only necessary because law foreclosed legitimate options — Woodcourt wants to give Magdalen and secondary characters more genuine agency; this is a direct and productive clash worth surfacing early

Hartley's claim that Collins REFUSES sentiment directly contradicts Woodcourt's entire reading strategy, which is grounded in emotional truth and felt experience — the host should name this tension explicitly once both positions are on the table

Blackstone's strongest take (injustice is never resolved, the system isn't fixed) actually aligns with Hartley's formal argument (Collins withholds narrative resolution just as law withholds identity) — if they realise they agree on the ending, that's a genuinely interesting moment

All three experts want to quote legal language passages but for different reasons: Blackstone wants the cold machinery, Woodcourt wants the suffocating sound, Hartley wants the information-rationing structure — reading the same passage together and asking each to say what they hear could be a strong radio moment

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that Magdalen's false self is actually *more vivid* on the page than her real one. Which specific moment in the text made you feel that most strongly? Because that seems like it should disturb us more than it does.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to cite a specific passage illustrating her prose-style argument, and set up the question of whether Magdalen even *has* a true self — which directly challenges Caroline's and James's frameworks

questions.question: Caroline, you said Magdalen is actually the *most honest* character in the whole novel — which sounds almost deliberately provocative. Can you defend that? Because James is already giving me a look.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to articulate her radical-honesty argument in full, and use the direct call-out to Blackstone to prime the disagreement about whether this is agency or adaptation

questions.question: James, you told me before we started that the mask is 'the only authentic thing she possesses' — but Eleanor is essentially saying there's no authentic thing underneath *at all*. Are you two actually agreeing, or is there a real fight here about what authenticity even means for Magdalen?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's legal-erasure framework and Hartley's epistemological one — they sound compatible but the implications are different, and prodding them to argue it out will clarify both positions

questions.question: Caroline, you mentioned wanting to find the moment where the mask *slips* — where Collins lets Magdalen be real. Did you find one? Because Eleanor's whole argument is that Collins deliberately makes that impossible. So either you found a crack in her theory, or you didn't find what you were looking for.
questions.intent: Create a direct test-case moment — either Caroline produces a passage that challenges Eleanor's thesis, or she concedes the point, either of which is good radio; targets the vulnerability/mask-slip passages Caroline flagged

questions.question: James, here's the thing I want to push on — if Magdalen's deception is purely rational adaptation to a legal system that's already erased her, does that let Collins off the hook? Like, does framing it as *structural* actually flatten her into a symbol rather than a person? Caroline's going to say yes.
questions.intent: Destabilize Blackstone's structural argument by raising the characterization question, and explicitly cue Caroline's pushback to keep the three-way tension alive into the end of the segment

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension that doesn't need much forcing — Blackstone reads structurally/legally, Hartley reads formally/epistemologically, Woodcourt reads psychologically/sympathetically. The goal is to get all three frameworks colliding on the *same passages* rather than talking past each other. Push everyone toward the text whenever possible. The most productive disagreement is probably Hartley vs. Woodcourt on whether a 'real' Magdalen exists at all — that's the one with genuine stakes for readers. Let it breathe. Blackstone and Woodcourt agree on sympathy but disagree on why, which is also worth surfacing. Keep the tone warm but don't let anyone stay too abstract for more than thirty seconds.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that Collins makes a 'true self' impossible directly contradicts Woodcourt's desire to find the mask-slip moment — get them arguing over a specific passage rather than general principles

Blackstone says deception is 'mandatory not liberated'; Woodcourt says it's an expression of radical agency — this is a direct clash that neither of them has fully acknowledged yet, and it needs a question that names it explicitly

Woodcourt's 'most honest character' argument actually supports Blackstone's legal-fiction framework in a way neither of them will expect — point this out and see if they're alarmed or pleased by the alliance

Hartley's prose-style argument (conditional clauses, nested revelations) is the one most likely to get skipped if the legal and psychological arguments dominate — make sure she gets a moment to actually read a sentence aloud and demonstrate what she means

questions.question: Caroline, you said in your notes that the prose actually *sings* when Wragge speaks — that there's a musicality to his syntax. Can you just read us one of those speeches? Pick the one where you think it hits hardest, and let's hear what you mean.
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to do a live read that demonstrates Wragge's verbal excess before the panel theorises about it — grounds the conversation in the actual text and sets a high-energy opening

questions.question: Eleanor, you've described Wragge's language as the con itself — the elaborate sentences are a kind of defence mechanism, a verbal shell game. But here's what I want to push on: are we laughing *at* something Collins intends to be funny, or are we being played? Is Collins conning *us* through Wragge?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's strongest and most unsettling take — that the reader is the real mark — and create the moment where the comedy tips into something darker

questions.question: James, I suspect you're itching to rain on the parade a bit here — because both Eleanor and Caroline are talking about Wragge as this almost admirable verbal genius, and you seem to want to say: hold on, these cons *actually worked* on real people and real institutions. Make the case.
questions.intent: Set up the direct friction between Blackstone's institutional-failure reading and Woodcourt/Hartley's more character-centred delight — provoke him to be the sceptic in the room

questions.question: You've got a passage in mind where Wragge pulls off a con against a respectable institution — false credentials, social performance, the whole thing. Can you read it and tell us: what is Collins actually documenting here about how Victorian law *failed*?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to anchor his institutional argument in a specific textual moment and demonstrate that the comedy has a forensic quality — moves the segment from character appreciation to structural critique

questions.question: Caroline, you said something that I keep coming back to — that Wragge is the only character in the whole novel who has no internal conflict whatsoever. No shame, no self-doubt, completely himself. In a book full of women being torn apart by duty and desire, does that make him *the freest character Collins wrote*? And should we find that troubling or enviable?
questions.intent: Set up the sharpest potential disagreement of the segment — Woodcourt finds Wragge's freedom almost radical, Blackstone will want to call it monstrous, and Hartley will complicate both by asking what it means that we envy him at all

steering_notes: Open with the live reading — let the text do its work before anyone theorises. The real energy in this segment comes from the tension between two things the guests all half-agree on: Wragge is delightful AND Wragge is dangerous. Don't let them resolve that tension too early. Keep pushing on the reader-complicity angle that Hartley raised — the idea that Collins is conning the audience through him is the most radio-friendly and genuinely unsettling thread. Blackstone is the natural disruptor here; use him to stop the panel getting too cosy about how charming Wragge is. End on the freedom-versus-monstrousness question — it's unresolvable in a satisfying way and will leave listeners with something to chew on.
cross_engagement_targets: Woodcourt says Wragge is 'completely himself' with no internal conflict — Blackstone will want to reframe that freedom as sociopathy rather than liberation; push them to talk directly to each other on this

Hartley's claim that Collins is more interested in the *technique* of the con than the moral condemnation sits in direct tension with Blackstone's insistence that the fraud had real victims — this is the segment's best disagreement and should be named out loud

Woodcourt reads Wragge as Magdalen's mirror (same amoral adaptability, different target); Hartley reads him as making the reader complicit — these are complementary but point in opposite directions about *who* the con is really being played on, and that's worth surfacing explicitly

segment_name: Noel's Inheritance: Plot, Property, and Powerlessness

questions.question: Caroline, you've called this novel a 'rage document disguised as a page-turner.' I love that. But let's start with the basics for anyone who hasn't read it — when Noel Vanstone shows up on the page, what are we actually looking at? Is he a villain, a victim, or something weirder than either of those?
questions.intent: Get the emotional stakes on the table fast, frame Noel as a contested figure, and set up Blackstone's structural reading against Woodcourt's emotional realism

questions.question: James, I can hear you itching to jump in there. Because your take is actually that Noel being contemptible or sympathetic is almost beside the point — the law made him irrelevant before he opened his mouth. Can you walk us through what the inheritance mechanics actually *do* to the people around him? What's the trap that's already been sprung before the novel even starts?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to lay out the legal-structural argument clearly, set up his 'institutional violence' frame, and give Hartley something formal to respond to

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to push on something. James is saying the inheritance mechanics *are* the point — understand the property law, understand the powerlessness. But you've told me you think Collins actually makes the mechanics deliberately confusing. That she *chooses* obscurity. So which is it — is the law the engine of the novel, or is the fog around it the engine?
questions.intent: Directly provoke the Blackstone-Hartley disagreement about whether clarity or opacity is Collins's method; get Hartley to make the 'form is content' argument

questions.question: Caroline, you mentioned you want to read the passage where the terms of Noel's will first land on the page — the conditional language, the legal restrictions. Can you read a bit of that now? Because I want everyone to react to the actual *sound* of it — does it feel like a document, or does it feel like something else?
questions.intent: Get a passage read aloud to ground the abstract argument in text; create a moment where all three experts respond to the same prose, likely disagreeing about what the sound *means*

questions.question: Eleanor, last one and I want to end on this — you said something in our conversation that's been rattling around in my head. You said Collins performs intimacy with Noel while keeping us at arm's length through formal technique. That we *think* we're inside her, but maybe we're not. If that's true, what does it mean that we're all so ready to root for her? Are we rooting for a character, or are we rooting for a grammatical effect?
questions.intent: Push Hartley to her sharpest formal claim and give Woodcourt — who believes in Collins's emotional realism — the maximum possible thing to disagree with; end on a genuinely unresolved question

steering_notes: The big tension in this segment is between Blackstone's structural-legal reading, Hartley's formalist reading, and Woodcourt's emotional-realist reading — and the good news is all three can be *right* and still productively fight. Don't let the conversation get too abstract too early; anchor every big claim in what the text actually does on the page. Woodcourt is the best person to keep bringing it back to emotional stakes when the other two go theoretical. If Blackstone and Hartley start talking past each other about whether the law or the prose is the 'real' subject, intervene with a 'but what does Magdalen *feel* in this moment' redirect to Woodcourt. The passage read-aloud in question 4 is the segment's centrepiece — give it room to breathe and don't rush the reactions.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone argues the inheritance mechanics must be understood clearly to understand the powerlessness — Hartley argues Collins *deliberately* obscures the mechanics and the obscurity is the meaning. This is a direct contradiction and should be surfaced explicitly around question 3.

Hartley suspects our access to Noel's interiority is shallower than it feels — Woodcourt believes Collins's prose rhythms produce genuine emotional realism and recognition. These two are talking about the same sentences and drawing opposite conclusions. Flag this when Woodcourt responds to the will passage in question 4.

Blackstone reads Noel Vanstone as a casualty of a system — neither villain nor victim but an irrelevance produced by law. Woodcourt and Hartley both risk reading him as simply weak or contemptible. Watch for this and let Blackstone correct it when it surfaces.

segment_name: Atmosphere of Intrigue: Collins's Suspenseful Craft

questions.question: Eleanor, you've said Collins invents a new kind of suspense in this book — not plot machinery, but something structural, almost architectural. Can you point us to a specific moment in the text where you feel that most sharply? Where the *form* itself is doing the frightening?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read and unpack a specific passage demonstrating fragmented narration or withheld information, establishing her 'formal invention' thesis early so Blackstone and Woodcourt can push back

questions.question: James, I can already hear you wanting to jump in there — because your take is almost the opposite, isn't it? You'd say we can't separate the suspense from the specific injustices Collins is depicting. So when Magdalen realizes the marriage certificate can be used *against* her — that the legal system is the trap — is that a thriller moment, or is that something else entirely?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's 'testimony not entertainment' thesis and directly challenge Hartley's formalism — provoke a disagreement about whether structure serves politics or stands alone

questions.question: Caroline, you've got a slightly different angle on both of these — you're interested in the *texture* of the prose, the hesitations in dialogue, the things characters won't say out loud. Can you give us an example of that? A moment where what goes *unsaid* is where the dread actually lives?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to read a passage featuring indirect dialogue or veiled menace, bridging Hartley's formal argument and Blackstone's political one while introducing the gendered dimension of powerlessness

questions.question: Here's something I want to put to all three of you, but Caroline I'll start with you — you've said social propriety isn't just a constraint in this book, it's actually *cover* for predatory behavior. That the rules of Victorian politeness make Nora more vulnerable, not less. Does that mean Collins is saying the everyday is the real danger? That the domestic surface is the horror?
questions.intent: Introduce the complicity-of-normality theme to force a three-way exchange — Hartley will want to connect this to domestic detail becoming sinister, Blackstone will want to push toward institutional critique

questions.question: James, final push from me — Eleanor would say the genius is structural, Caroline would say it's emotional and gendered. You're saying it's none of those things in isolation: it's *testimony*. Victorian readers would have felt this as documentary, not sensation fiction. Do you think that still works on a modern reader, or has that urgency faded? Can we still feel what Collins intended us to feel?
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to defend the contemporary relevance of his political reading and give Hartley and Woodcourt a chance to agree or complicate — good closing energy for the segment

steering_notes: Keep pushing the three-way tension between form (Hartley), politics (Blackstone), and emotional/gendered experience (Woodcourt) — these aren't incompatible readings but the experts will instinctively defend their territory, which makes for good radio. Don't let anyone get too abstract; always redirect to a specific passage or moment in the text. The most productive flashpoint is probably the marriage certificate scene and the question of whether that moment is structurally clever, politically radical, or emotionally devastating — ideally, get all three to weigh in on the same passage from different angles. Watch for Woodcourt and Hartley finding unexpected common ground on the domestic-detail-as-menace point, which might actually isolate Blackstone productively.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that suspense is 'formal invention' directly contradicts Blackstone's insistence that structure only matters because it serves a political indictment — push them to name what they think the *purpose* of Collins's technique actually is

Woodcourt's argument that propriety enables predatory behavior complements Blackstone's institutional critique but comes from a completely different angle (emotional/gendered vs. legal/systemic) — get them to figure out if they're actually agreeing

Hartley's focus on 'epistemic darkness' shared by reader and protagonist overlaps significantly with Woodcourt's point about complicity in characters' uncertainty — they may not realize how close they are, and the moment they do could be the segment's best exchange

Blackstone's dismissal of the 'proto-thriller' reading is a direct challenge to Hartley's formalism — if she hears it as an attack on style-over-substance, she'll push back hard, which is exactly what you want

segment_name: No Name, No Identity: Thematic Syntheses

questions.question: Caroline, you said in our chat beforehand that the real subject of this novel isn't identity at all — it's shame. That's a pretty provocative reframe. Can you sell me on that? Because when I read it, I kept thinking about legal status, about what a name actually does in Victorian society. What makes you land on shame as the centre of gravity?
questions.intent: Open with Caroline's most distinctive and provocative take to immediately signal this won't be a conventional 'identity in Victorian literature' discussion — and to give Blackstone something to respond to

questions.question: James, I have to bring you in here, because your whole argument is basically the opposite — that this is institutional critique, not emotional texture. Are you saying Collins is less interested in what Magdalen feels than in what the law is doing to her? Because Caroline's going to push back hard on that.
questions.intent: Force the Blackstone-Woodcourt disagreement into the open early — 'institutional machinery vs. felt experience' is a genuinely productive tension and they clearly have incompatible readings of what the novel is FOR

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring in the passage you mentioned where another character looks straight at Magdalen and fails to recognise her — because you read that as Collins saying identity is purely social construction, not essential truth. But Blackstone would say that's the law doing its work, and Caroline would say that's the shame made visible. Who's right? Or is the passage doing all three things at once?
questions.intent: Use a specific textual moment to triangulate all three positions simultaneously — get the passage read aloud and then let all three experts fight over what it actually proves

questions.question: Eleanor, your strongest claim is that at the end of this novel, Magdalen is renamed but not restored — that marriage and legal resolution don't actually put her back together. That sounds like you're saying Collins wrote a quietly devastating ending that most readers mistake for a happy one. Is that right? And how does the form of the novel — the structure, the withholding — actually make that argument for him?
questions.intent: Draw out Hartley's formal reading in full, particularly her claim about the ending as structurally radical rather than sentimentally reassuring — sets up a three-way argument about what the ending is doing

questions.question: James, final question for you — and I want the others to weigh in too. You said we should feel outrage at specific laws that actually existed when we read this novel. That's a big claim about what fiction is for. Do Eleanor and Caroline think Collins would agree with you? Because one of them thinks the legal plot is almost beside the point, and the other thinks the book is fundamentally about comedy and irony rather than outrage. Is there actually a single novel here, or are you all reading three different books?
questions.intent: Close the segment with a genuine methodological disagreement about how to read the novel and what fiction does — force the question of whether their interpretations are complementary or actually incompatible

steering_notes: The productive fault line here is Blackstone's institutional reading versus Woodcourt's phenomenological one, with Hartley's formal argument cutting across both. Resist the temptation to let them find easy consensus — they actually disagree about what the novel is fundamentally FOR, and that's worth keeping live. Push back if anyone retreats into 'well, Collins is doing all of these things' — make them commit. The ending is the flashpoint: all three have distinct and incompatible readings of whether it's redemption, indictment, or formal sleight of hand. Save that for the back half. Keep energy conversational — the goal is for listeners to feel the argument, not follow a thesis.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone says the legal plot is the substance; Hartley says it's scaffolding — they need to be put in direct dialogue on this point, ideally over a specific passage where the law's verdict becomes narrative fact

Woodcourt's claim that Collins is funny about Victorian respectability in ways that undercut the sentimental reading directly challenges both Blackstone's outrage-driven reading and Hartley's modernist-fragmentation reading — get her to make that comedy case explicitly and watch the others react

All three have a reading of the ending: Hartley says renamed-not-restored, Blackstone says indictment-not-redemption, Woodcourt says shame-domesticated-not-resolved — these are close enough to look similar but different enough to generate genuine argument if pushed
